paper_title: The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs, and the most accurate SOTA model is a fit, not a law: it absorbs architecture into fitted coefficients, requiring per-LLM fitting. We derive closed-form expressions of the computational and memory-access complexity of LLM inference in terms of architectural hyperparameters, covering MHA and GQA, and compare a family of analytical models of increasing granularity. From these, we obtain the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache cost and next-token computation. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from six families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1-3.5x below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration. The SIMPLE law explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with the hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and more aggressive GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy by up to 3x relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; although accuracy grows with the budget, energy grows faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x reasoning-budget range. Agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0x relative to non-agentic ones, driven by the growth of both the prefill and the KV-cache terms with input length; while prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%), the KV-cache term is unaffected, so even a cached agentic request costs 4.8x more.

Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving superlinear energy growth; although accuracy grows with the budget, energy grows faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14 across 4.0 reasoning-budget range. An interactive implementation of SIMPLE is available at ecs-lab/SIMPLE. 1. Introduction Inference, not training, is where most of the energy of Large Language Model (LLM) is spent: model is trained once and then served continuously, and inference accounts for up to 90% of its life-cycle energy [15]. Yet for an LLM not yet deployed, the only dependable way to know that cost is to build it, serve it, and measure it, an answer that arrives once the architecture is no longer choice. The target is also moving: reasoning spends additional tokens to buy accuracy [21], while agentic workflows [7] have pushed median prompt lengths from 7501050 to 68K tokens [18]. The token is the unit of account of this economy. Inference is priced, billed, budgeted, and benchmarked per token [35], and capacity is planned in tokens per second and tokens per joule. Yet no analytical model states what token costs, and no law names the factors that set it. token is an observable of the workload, not unit of computational work: each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so average token energy depends on input length, generation length, context reuse, and how attention is organized. An entire industry settles in currency whose production cost cannot be computed. Energy models exhibit the same gap in analytical form. Prior work fits energy as function of input and output lengths [38, 43, 40, 24] empirically, without deriving it from the computational kernels, thereby describing measured regime rather than explaining it. SweetSpot [26], the most accurate analytical formulation reported to date, removes the decisive obstacle by deriving the decode phase in closed form from the computation and memory accesses of decoder-only Transformer inference. SweetSpot, however, is fit, not law. Its coefficients are identified on single LLM and carry that LLMs architecture implicitly: the number of layers, the hidden dimension, and the organization of attention never appear as terms. The formulation therefore neither names the factors that set the cost of token nor applies to model it has not already measured, and later analytical models [36, 11, 22] relax this only in part. This limitation is felt where decisions are now being made: in energy efficiency. Intelligence per Watt relates delivered capability to the power that produced it [27], and serving is reported in tokens per joule [35], but both are measured on systems that already exist. sections.content: after the fact and cannot say which architecture would deliver the same capability for less, how many reasoning tokens are worth spending [21], or at what context length serving an agentic request ceases to be affordable [18]. measured efficiency locates no optimum. What is therefore needed is law expressed in the architectures own hyperparameters, one that explains which of them govern the energy of token, predicts that energy for an LLM never benchmarked, and thereby turns efficiency from something observed into something derived. Modern LLMs share the decoder-only Transformer [37] and differ in handful of hyperparameters and attention architectures: Multi-Head Attention (MHA) has largely given way to Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) [1] and Multihead Latent Attention (MLA) [9], each cutting memory traffic and KV-cache size, and with them the energy per generated token [26]. Furthermore, long generations, 68Ktoken contexts, and mandatory prefix caching push todays requests precisely into the regime where the KV-cache term dominates: no law of token cost can be blind to how attention is organized. Together, these considerations motivate the following open research questions: RQ1: Is there an analytical model that can accurately predict inference energy across LLMs with different architectures, including the attention mechanism? RQ2: Can an LLM-agnostic model remain compact and accurate enough to be practical alternative to LLM-specific models, while generalizing to unseen LLM architectures and workloads? RQ3: How do LLM size and architectural hyperparameters influence inference energy consumption? RQ4: How does the reasoning token budget affect inference energy and Intelligence per Joule? RQ5: How does the energy cost of single query shift from non-agentic to agentic workloads? This work answers these with the following contributions: We present taxonomy of state-of-the-art LLM inference energy models, classified by functional form, grounding theory, and ability to predict inference energy across LLMs with different architectures, including the attention mechanism. We find that the most accurate model, SweetSpot [26], absorbs architectural information implicitly into its fitted coefficients, requiring per-LLM calibration and making it neither LLM-agnostic nor attention-aware. The SOTA therefore lacks an analytical model capable of accurately predicting the energy consumed by generic request for an arbitrary LLM. To close this gap, we analytically derive closed-form expressions for the computational and memory-access complexity of LLM inference, covering both MHA and GQA mechanisms Building on these, we propose the SIMPLE law, which separately models prefill and decode energy costs, further decomposing the latter into the self-attention KV-cache cost and the next-token computation (i.e., the feed-forward network). Validated against family of analytically derived models spanning different fitting granularities and modeling approaches, SIMPLE achieves the best accuracy-compactness trade-off among the evaluated models, reducing the error of SOTA models by 3.1 3.5. Applying the SIMPLE law across LLMs of different sizes, families, and architectures, we show that hidden dimension 𝑑 is the most sensitive architectural hyperparameter, as prefill energy scales quadratically with 𝑑, while layer depth contributes linearly. Attention architecture matters strongly: more aggressive GQA KV grouping reduces per-token energy by up to 3 relative to standard MHA, making it an impactful architectural choice for reducing inference energy. We use the SIMPLE law to analytically derive the that minimizes per-token energy output length 𝜏𝑜𝑢𝑡 (the sweet spot), showing that increasing the reasoning token budget pushes 𝜏𝑜𝑢𝑡 beyond this minimum, driving super-linear energy growth. Although accuracy grows with the reasoning budget, energy grows faster, so Intelligence Per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14 at the lowest and highest budgets across 4.0 range. Using the SIMPLE law, we analyze the energy cost of agentic AI workloads and show that energy per request increases by 13.0 relative to non-agentic ones, driven by the growth of both the prefill and KVcache terms with input length. While prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%), the KV-cache term, accounting for 86% of the remaining energy, is unaffected, so even cached agentic request still costs 4.8 more than non-agentic one. We evaluate our models on large dataset [26] of TensorRT-LLM [23] traces collected from set of widely used dense LLMs running on NVIDIA H100. The included models span model sizes and architectures, covering OPT [44], LLaMA [14], Gemma [33], Falcon [2], Qwen2 [41], and Granite [20]. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. After providing background in Section 2, we review related work in Section 3. Then we derive the floating point and memory operations of LLM inference in Section 4, and building on this, we present in Section 5 SIMPLE, together with the family of complexity-derived models used throughout the evaluation. In Section 6 we experimentally validate SIMPLE, and discuss in Section 7 how model size, architectural hyperparameters, reasoning, and agentic workloads impact energy consumption. Finally, we conclude in Section 8. H. Pizzini Cavagna, A. Proia et al.: Preprint submitted to Elsevier Page 2 of

sections.content: 2. Background This section introduces the background needed for the analysis in this work. We briefly review the fundamentals of LLM architectures, their computational characteristics, and the metrics used throughout the paper. LLM Architecture LLMs are built on the Transformer architecture [37], which has become the standard for generative AI. Transformer block consists of two main components, the Multi-Head Self-Attention Mechanism (MHA) and the Feed-Forward Network (FFN), each wrapped in residual connections, layer normalization, and dropout. In MHA, the hidden representation is projected into several subspaces, corresponding to different heads. Each head learns to capture different type of dependency within the sequence, and the head outputs are then combined. This improves the models expressivity and its ability to represent diverse relationships, but it also increases the number of operations in proportion to the number of heads. To reduce this overhead, Multi-Query Attention (MQA) was proposed in 2019 [29]. It keeps multiple query heads but shares single set of Key-Value (KV) projections across all of them, which drastically reduces memory usage and KV-cache size during decoding and makes inference more efficient. More recently, Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) was introduced in 2023 [1] as generalization of MHA and MQA: keys and values are shared within groups of heads, striking balance between the efficiency of MQA and the expressivity of MHA. Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), introduced with DeepSeek-V2 [9], provides different mechanism to reduce the KV-cache footprint. Rather than sharing KV projections across heads, it compresses keys and values into single lowrank latent vector. The full per-head keys and values are then recovered from this latent through up-projection matrices, preserving the expressivity of MHA at fraction of the memory cost. Despite its distinct compression mechanism, MLA can nonetheless be seen as variant of GQA [5]. LLM Inference Computation In large-scale models, most of the learnable weights, referred to as parameters, reside in the FFN layers, whereas the runtime complexity is dominated by the attention mechanism, owing to its quadratic dependence on the input sequence length. The total number of parameters, typically in the billions, is referred to as model size. LLM inference is typically split into two phases: prefill, in which the entire input sequence is processed in parallel to initialize the KV-cache, and decode, in which tokens are generated autoregressively [42]. During prefill, the computational cost is dominated by the quadratic attention term; during decode, thanks to the reuse of cached keys and values, the cost per token grows only linearly with the sequence length. Nevertheless, for long outputs, the decode phase often accounts for most of the total inference time, since tokens must be produced one at time, which restricts the opportunities for parallelization. On modern GPUs, the throughput of LLM inference is constrained not only by arithmetic performance but also by memory bandwidth. Storing and retrieving the large KVcache during decoding places considerable stress on the memory subsystem. For example, in autoregressive decoding, every generated token requires loading all previous keys and values from memory, which makes attention kernels strongly memory-bound, especially for long contexts. Metrics and Measurement We define the total energy consumption 𝐸tot(𝜏in, 𝜏out), expressed in Joules, as the energy the GPU consumes to process given request, characterized by an input length 𝜏in and an output length 𝜏out. Normalizing 𝐸tot by 𝜏out yields the Energy-per-Token 𝐸tok: 𝐸tok = 𝐸tot 𝜏out ] [ Joules Token We also define energy efficiency 𝐸eff as the reciprocal of 𝐸tok, capturing the number of output tokens generated per unit of energy. Finally, to relate energy consumption to the quality of the generated output, we adopt the Intelligence per Joule (IPJ) metric [27]. We compute it as the ratio of task accuracy to the energy required to process request: IPJ = Acc 𝐸tot [ Accuracy % Joule ] where Acc is the accuracy averaged over the evaluated queries and 𝐸tot is the average per-request energy, making it practical metric for realistic deployment scenarios. 3. Related Work Recent work on LLM inference energy falls broadly into two categories: (i) experimental characterization of energy consumption, and (ii) analytical or empirical models for predicting it. We review each in turn, then position our contributions with respect to the identified limitations. 3.1. Experimental Characterizations Several studies have characterized LLM inference energy across different workloads and hardware conditions. Samsi et al. [28] benchmark energy for LLaMA models of varying sizes across two NVIDIA GPU generations (V100 and A100), including multi-node and multi-GPU execution. Chung et al. [6] introduce ML.ENERGY, benchmark suite for measuring energy under realistic serving conditions across different tasks, and show that automated configuration recommendations can reduce consumption. Stojkovic et al. [31] study how inference server configurations affect latency, throughput, and energy. Maliakel et al. [19] examine the effect of GPU Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) settings on energy for different workloads. Fernandez et al. [13] analyze energy across inference optimization strategies and task types. Wilhelm et al. [39] investigate the accuracyenergy trade-off, focusing on how inference strategies such as chain-of-thought affect it. Unlike the following works, none of these proposes an energy prediction model. sections.content: 3.2. Predictive Models Recent studies have proposed models to predict the energy consumption of LLM inference. These models focus on the number of input and output tokens (𝜏in and 𝜏out), while not explicitly accounting for batch size. Batch size is instead commonly incorporated into models targeting distributed inference [17, 25], whereas it is generally not considered in models for single-GPU inference, as in our setting. The following paragraphs review the state-of-the-art models, grouped by 𝐸tot functional form and further characterized by three criteria that directly reflect the limitations our work addresses. First, whether they are analytically derived from first principles, such as Transformer computational complexity, or are empirical. Second, whether they must be fitted separately for each LLM. We refer to models that require per-LLM fit as LLM-specific, and to those that do not as LLM-agnostic. Third, whether they are attentionaware, meaning that they explicitly account for different attention mechanisms, rather than assuming standard MHA. Table 1 summarizes all reviewed models along these criteria. Linear Models common empirical approach is to assign fixed cost to input and output sequence lengths, yielding linear model: 𝐸tot 𝜃0 + 𝜃1𝜏in + 𝜃2𝜏out Both Vellaisamy et al. [38] and Zhan et al. [43] propose linear models, though they differ in how they handle inputlength dependence. Vellaisamy et al. focuses solely on decode energy absorbing the prefill cost into fixed constant, effectively modeling decode energy as linear in 𝜏out alone, while Zhan et al. make 𝜏in an explicit term as in the formulation above. Neither model is derived from first principles or includes architectural hyperparameters, so both must be fitted separately for each LLM and are not attention-aware. Zhan et al. [43] apply their model to Vision-Language Models and additionally propose an LLM-agnostic formulation that scales with model size 𝑆 (in billions of parameters): 𝐸tot 𝜃0 + 𝜃1𝑆 + 𝜃2𝜏in + 𝜃3𝜏out + 𝜃4𝑆𝜏in + 𝜃5𝑆𝜏out While this formulation is LLM-agnostic, model size serves as the only architectural proxy, capturing scale but not structural hyperparameters such as the number of layers, hidden dimension, or attention configuration. Bilinear Models Wilkins et al. [40] and Delavande et al. [11] extend the linear formulation with an interaction term between input and output sequence lengths: 𝐸tot 𝜃0 + 𝜃1 𝜏in + 𝜃2 𝜏out + 𝜃3 𝜏in𝜏out Wilkins et al. motivate the interaction term statistically, using ANOVA to confirm that input and output lengths have significant joint effect on energy, and fit the model empirically via ordinary least squares. Delavande et al. derive the same form analytically from the roofline model: the interaction term reflects the cumulative cost of attending to growing context at each decode step. Neither model includes architectural hyperparameters, thus both must be fitted separately for each LLM and are not attention-aware. Power-law Models Oviedo et al. [24] propose bottomup framework that estimates per-query inference energy from node power draw and token throughput: 𝐸tot = PUE 3.6 𝑃node 𝐿eff TPS(𝜏in, 𝜏out) where PUE accounts for data-center overhead, 𝑃node is the measured steady-state node power, TPS(𝜏in, 𝜏out) is fitted empirically to per-model benchmarks as piecewise loglinear regression, and 𝐿eff 𝜏out scales energy by output length. Because TPS is linear in log 𝜏in and log 𝜏out, substituting it into the formula yields power-law dependence on sequence lengths: 𝐸tot 𝜃0 𝜏𝜃1 in 𝜏𝜃2 out The framework includes no architectural hyperparameters; thus the throughput model must be re-fitted for each LLM, making the approach LLM-specific and not attention-aware. sections.content: Quadratic Models SweetSpot [26] models inference energy as proportional to FLOPs and data transfers, analytically derived from the transformer computational kernels as function of 𝜏in and 𝜏out. The decoding phase is handled by expressing the growing KV-cache context as an arithmetic series, which yields closed-form quadratic formulation: 𝐸tot 𝜃0 + 𝜃1 𝜏in + 𝜃2 𝜏2 in + 𝜃3 𝜏in𝜏out + 𝜃4 𝜏out + 𝜃5 𝜏2 out The model reduces the MAPE of the bilinear baseline from over 30% to below 2%. However, the fitted coefficients are LLM-specific, requiring an exhaustive measurement dataset for each target model. The approach therefore cannot generalize to unseen architectures or be applied during training. Moreover, the analytical derivation treats all 𝑄, 𝐾, and 𝑉 projection matrices as having the same hidden dimension 𝑑, implicitly assuming standard MHA. Since the attention mechanism is not parameterized in the formulation, SweetSpot is not attention-aware. Following similar analytical approach, Vartziotis et al. [36] decompose inference energy into compute and memory-access components: 𝐸tot 𝛼TC 𝐶TC + 𝑒HBM 𝐵 𝜂(𝑁) where 𝐶TC denotes the total tensor-core FLOP count for prefill and decode, and 𝐵 denotes the total HBM traffic. 𝐶TC and 𝐵 are derived analytically from the transformer computational graph, following similar decomposition to [26], though the FLOP count 𝐶TC relies on the Kaplan training parameter-scaling approximation [16] (𝐶 𝐾𝑁𝑇 , 𝐾 = 6 FLOPs per parameter per token) rather than an inference kernel-by-kernel tally. The factor 𝜂(𝑁), where 𝑁 is the number of model hyperparameters, is dimensionless inefficiency multiplier that accounts for non-ideal HBM bandwidth utilization, while 𝛼TC and 𝑒HBM are hardware-specific energy coefficients for tensor-core and HBM operations, expressed in pJ/FLOP and pJ/bit respectively (H100 GPU, FP16/BF16). Because 𝛼TC and 𝑒HBM are hardware constants rather than fitted per-model coefficients, and 𝐶TC and 𝐵 are expressed in terms of 𝑁 and structural hyperparameters such as layer count and hidden dimension, the model is LLMagnostic and captures the order-of-magnitude energy and scaling trends observed in authors measurements. However, its accuracy is limited, with reported mean relative error of approximately 20%. Furthermore, expanding 𝐶TC and 𝐵 yields long closed-form expression in the architectural hyperparameters, which makes the model hard to interpret and limits its usefulness for identifying the hyperparameters that drive energy consumption. Similarly to SweetSpot, the model assumes MHA, so the reduced KVcache traffic of GQA, which is standard in many modern LLMs, is not captured by the model. To the best of our knowledge, Niu et al. [22] is the only existing work to propose an attention-aware energy model for LLM inference. Their model estimates the energy per output token of single decode step, expressing decode energy as linear function of the bytes accessed, considering RQ1: Is there an analytical model that can accurately predict inference energy across LLMs with different architectures, including the attention mechanism? No. The most accurate model, SweetSpot [26], is LLMspecific: its coefficients must be fitted for each target LLM, so it cannot generalize to unseen architectures. LLM-agnostic alternatives do not explicitly model the attention mechanism; the most analytically grounded of these [36] reports mean relative error of about 20% and yields hard-to-interpret expressions. The one model that parameterizes the attention mechanism [22] targets the decode phase only and requires measured runtime inputs, making it inapplicable to total inference energy prediction. No prior model is simultaneously interpretable, LLM-agnostic, attention-aware, and applicable to the full inference pipeline. SIMPLE is the first to satisfy all these conditions. both the model weights and the KV-cache, and the measured decode time. The KV-cache byte term is analytically derived from the model architecture and attention mechanism: it is explicitly parametrized by the number of KV heads per layer (𝑁𝑘𝑣 ), which accounts for MHA and GQA. The decode time, however, must be measured at runtime. The resulting model requires separate calibration and fit for each LLM and hardware configuration. Since the model covers only the decode phase energy, excluding the prefill, it is not directly applicable to predict the total inference energy 𝐸tot for given query, which is the focus of this work. We therefore do not consider it further here. 3.3. SIMPLE Model The box above summarizes the answer to RQ1. We address the key limitations of previous approaches by extending the derivation of the computational and memoryaccess complexities of SweetSpot [26] to GQA, and using the resulting expressions to derive SIMPLE, compact LLM-agnostic model that explicitly represents the attention mechanism, builds on SweetSpots interpretable quadratic structure to expose the role of individual architectural hyperparameters, and predicts energy across multiple LLM architectures without per-LLM calibration. Throughout our study, we target the Energy-per-Token 𝐸tok, rather than total energy consumption 𝐸tot, since normalizing by 𝜏out isolates the cost of generation from the cost of processing the input, exposing the trade-off between amortizing the prefill cost over more output tokens and incurring additional decode cost as 𝜏out grows. Moreover, 𝐸tok serves as natural unit for comparison across different workloads and deployments, as it corresponds directly to operational metrics such as cost-per-token and tokens-perjoule, matching how inference is commonly priced and provisioned in production. FLOPs and MemOPs Formulation In this section, we present the analytical derivation of the Floating-Point Operations (FLOPs) and Memory Operations (MemOPs) of LLM inference based on decoder-only Transformer, distinguishing the prefill and decode phases and assuming no quantization of weights or KV-cache. Experimental Validation This section details the experimental study conducted to validate SIMPLE. Section 6.1 describes the dataset 1 introduced in [26] and reused in our experiments, summarizing its key observations on energy consumption, namely the relevance of the attention mechanism and the non-linear relationship with input and output lengths. Section 6.2 presents our results 2. 6.1. Dataset Description The dataset contains energy measurements of TensorRTLLM inference traces collected from diverse set of widely used dense LLMs running on NVIDIA H100 accelerators. The included models span range of LLM sizes and architectures, including MHA and on GQA with different KV grouping ratios, using standard bf16 format for weights and KV-cache. The full list of models is given in Table 4. The dataset comprises synthetic requests processed using trtllm-bench configured in throughput mode, with request concurrency set to 1000 and maximum batch size of 1024. The maximum sequence length and the maximum number of batched tokens are both set to 8192. The experiments were conducted using one GPU per run on server equipped with an Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ CPU and four NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPUs connected via NVLink. Input and output lengths independently span 64 4096 tokens in powers of two, yielding 49 combinations with 1000 requests each. GPU power was sampled every 500 ms using pynvml [8]. The per-query energy was obtained by multiplying the average GPU power over 1000-request by the total measurement time, and dividing by the number of requests. Since neither the baseline models nor the SIMPLE model explicitly accounts for batching, we use these fixed settings, and fit energy per individual request. The box above summarizes the answer to RQ4. 7.3. Energy Cost in Agentic Workloads So far, SOTA works [11, 24, 12] have focused on evaluating the environmental impact of conversational AI. Agentic AI workloads are changing this landscape, and no existing work proposes theoretical framework that can capture and explain the resulting transformation in energy cost, as they lack way of accounting for prompt/prefix caching. Liu et al. [18] present an extensive analysis of the GitHub Copilot [7] coding agent production workload. Unlike conversational AI, characterized by queries with median prompt length (𝜏in) of 7501050 tokens and median completion length (𝜏out) of 80105, the reported agentic workload follows long-tail distribution with median context length (𝜏in) of 68K tokens and median completion length of 247 tokens. Moreover, they report median prefix KV-cache of 63K tokens, which corresponds to hit rate of 93%. This means that in the average query only 5K input tokens (out of 68K) are newly computed in the prefill stage. We apply the SIMPLE law with the following adaptation. Let 𝜏c 𝜏in be the number of input tokens served from the cache. Only the uncached suffix needs to be prefilled, so the Prefill Amortization term in the SIMPLE law ( 𝜃1 𝑑2𝐿 𝜏in𝜏out) scales with 𝜏in 𝜏c instead of 𝜏in. Table 8 quantifies this effect for Llama 3.1 8B on the median GitHub Copilot request, comparing three scenarios. In the non-agentic scenario, for which we consider only the non-cached input (𝜏in = 5K, 𝜏c = 0), the request costs 138.1 J, with Prefill (88.8 J) as the dominant term and the KV-cache contribution (43.2 J) playing secondary role. Moving to the agentic scenario (𝜏in = 68K, 𝜏c = 0), both context-dependent terms grow approximately proportionally to 𝜏in: Prefill increases by 13.6 and KV-cache by 13.3, while the Next-token term is unchanged, bringing 𝐸tot to 1787.7 (13.0). Prefix caching (𝜏in = 68K, 𝜏c = 63K) is highly effective on the Prefill term in this setting: only the 5K uncached tokens are processed, reducing Prefill contribution back to 88.8 (93%) and reducing 𝐸tot by 2.7 (668.7 J). However, the agentic cached request still consumes 4.8 more energy than the non-agentic one. This is because the KV-cache term is unaffected by prefix caching: the full 68K context must still be read and attended to at every decoding step, accounting for 86% of the remaining energy. Taken together, these results establish the SIMPLE law as an analytical foundation for sustainable LLM inference. Our approach is subject to few limitations, which we group into three categories. First, our evaluation is restricted to dense, single-GPU LLMs and does not cover mixture-ofexperts models. We also restrict our evaluation to MHA and GQA attention mechanisms; validation on more recent attention variants, LLM sizes, and architectures is left for future work. Second, the SIMPLE law does not explicitly model batch size or the number of concurrent requests as hyperparameters of the formulation. We plan to explicitly incorporate such additional workload parameters to extend the law. Finally, the reference dataset was collected using TensorRTLLM on single H100 GPU. Therefore, the SIMPLE law captures the energy behavior of single-device inference, and does not account for the additional costs of multi-GPU deployments, such as inter-device communication, tensor or pipeline parallelism, and distributed KV-cache management. As such, the fitted coefficients are specific to this hardwareframework pair. How the coefficients would change using other accelerators, multi-GPU deployments, and other inference frameworks remains to be explored in future work.
